Family Health

COVID-19 vaccines and Omicron: what the early comparisons showed

Updated: October 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

When Omicron emerged in late 2021, it changed how well the original COVID-19 vaccines prevented infection. Early studies found that booster doses improved immune responses and protection, especially against serious illness. This article explains those historical Pfizer, Moderna and Johnson & Johnson comparisons, distinguishes laboratory findings from clinical outcomes, and shows why current vaccine decisions need current local guidance.

Why the date of a vaccine comparison matters

The original Omicron reports were written while the variant was spreading rapidly and researchers were working with incomplete data. They discussed the vaccines, dose schedules and population immunity of late 2021 and early 2022. Those findings remain useful for understanding what happened, but they are not a ranking of the products available now.

At that time, two doses of an original mRNA vaccine, or one dose of the original Janssen vaccine, were often described as a completed primary course. The expression fully vaccinated therefore had a different practical meaning from being up to date with a later season’s recommendations.

A reported percentage belongs to a particular study. It depends on which outcome was measured, the variant, the participants, previous infection and time since vaccination. There is no single permanent percentage that describes a vaccine against every form of Omicron.

Omicron compared with Delta

Early Omicron studies found substantially more escape from protection against infection than had been seen with Delta. This helped explain why reinfections and infections in vaccinated people became more common, even when vaccination continued to reduce the risk of severe outcomes.

Imperial College London’s December 2021 analysis estimated that the relative risk of reinfection with Omicron was about 5.4 times that with Delta in the data it studied. That comparison was an early population estimate, not a prediction that an individual would be infected a fixed number of times.

The first reports also had too few hospital outcomes to settle how severe Omicron was relative to Delta. A statement that an early study found no clear difference did not prove equal severity. The estimate changed as follow-up and evidence accumulated.

Even a variant with a lower average risk of severe disease can put pressure on hospitals when it infects many people quickly. Transmission, the vulnerability of those infected and the size of the wave all matter alongside severity per infection.

Infection, symptoms and hospital admission are different outcomes

Protection against any detected infection is different from protection against symptomatic disease, hospital admission or death. A vaccine can offer limited protection against catching a variant while retaining more protection against a serious outcome.

Vaccine effectiveness generally describes a relative reduction in the measured outcome in a study population. For example, 70% effectiveness against admission does not mean that 30% of vaccinated people will be admitted. The underlying chance of admission and the comparison group matter.

Laboratory studies ask another question: how well do antibodies in a blood sample neutralise a virus or a laboratory version of it? Those studies can provide an early warning of immune escape, but they do not directly count hospitalisations or establish a person’s probability of infection.

Antibodies are also only part of immunity. Immune memory and cellular responses help explain why a reduction in measured neutralisation does not automatically mean the complete loss of protection against severe disease.

What two original Pfizer doses showed

In the first Omicron wave, two original Pfizer–BioNTech doses offered less protection against infection than they had against earlier variants. Early summaries often described modest protection against infection alongside stronger protection against hospital admission. The exact estimates differed with the study and time since dose two.

A South African analysis compared an Omicron-dominant period from November 15 to December 7, 2021, with an earlier Delta period. It estimated 70% effectiveness against hospital admission during the Omicron period, compared with 93% during the Delta period. The Omicron estimate had a 95% confidence interval of 62% to 76%.

These were observational data, not a trial in which participants were randomly assigned to encounter Delta or Omicron. Prior infection, changing testing patterns and the use of a period of variant dominance all matter when interpreting the results.

Early infection estimates sometimes quoted as roughly 30–40% should therefore not be used as a universal Pfizer protection level. They were not interchangeable with the hospitalisation result and did not describe protection at every point after vaccination.

Why a Pfizer booster changed the early picture

British data from the first Omicron wave showed a substantial increase in protection against symptomatic illness soon after an mRNA booster. Early estimates were around 70–75% in the first weeks, including people whose original course had been Pfizer or AstraZeneca.

The initial reports described slightly different results depending on the first vaccine series. Those differences did not establish that one sequence was permanently best. Follow-up duration and the characteristics of each group affected the estimates.

Later peer-reviewed analysis by Andrews and colleagues documented both improved protection after boosting and waning over time. A figure measured shortly after dose three could not be assumed to remain unchanged months later.

The practical historical finding was that an additional dose restored part of the protection lost through waning and immune escape. It did not make breakthrough infection impossible or establish that every person should follow the same three-dose schedule indefinitely.

What the antibody studies did and did not prove

Pfizer’s preliminary December 2021 laboratory reporting described a large reduction in Omicron neutralisation after two doses compared with the original virus, and a marked increase after a third dose. Published laboratory studies subsequently supported the general finding that boosting improved neutralising activity.

Researchers also compared blood samples from small groups of healthcare workers and other volunteers with different vaccination histories. Some reports described very large fold changes in antibody measurements. A fold change depends on the starting level, assay, sampling time and comparison being made.

A 25-fold difference in a laboratory measurement is not a 25-fold difference in a person’s chance of hospitalisation. Likewise, a striking increase after a booster does not mean that infection has become impossible. It is evidence of an immune response, which must be interpreted alongside clinical outcomes.

Comparing the largest fold change from one company or study with a smaller figure from another is not a fair head-to-head vaccine comparison. The methods and participants may be different, and neither result alone measures the whole immune response.

Severe illness and the early UK hospitalisation estimates

Early modelling suggested that boosters could preserve substantial protection against severe Omicron disease, although estimates relied on assumptions while clinical outcomes were still accumulating. A modelled percentage and a directly observed hospitalisation estimate should not be presented as the same kind of evidence.

The UK Health Security Agency’s first weekly vaccine-surveillance report of 2022 estimated effectiveness against Omicron hospitalisation at about 72% two to twenty-four weeks after dose two, 52% at twenty-five weeks or more, and 88% at least two weeks after a booster.

These figures combined analyses of protection against symptomatic disease and subsequent hospitalisation. They were estimates across vaccine brands in that analysis, rather than a clean result for Moderna alone or Pfizer alone. The confidence intervals and changing data also matter.

The historical pattern was stronger protection against admission after boosting than after an older two-dose course. Reusing 88% as a current guarantee, or labelling it as the fixed effectiveness of a particular brand, would overstate what the report established.

What the original Moderna studies showed

At the beginning of the Omicron wave, there was less clinical outcome information for Moderna than readers might expect from a product comparison. Small laboratory studies found substantially reduced neutralisation after the original two-dose course and stronger responses after a booster.

Preliminary reporting examined different booster amounts, including 50 and 100 micrograms. Widely reported increases of approximately 37-fold and more than 80-fold described antibody responses relative to pre-booster levels in those experiments. They did not establish equivalent percentage reductions in infection or hospital admission.

A subsequent published mRNA-1273 study examined serum from participants in the COVE trials and several booster formulations. Its focus was neutralisation, including the effect of dose and formulation. That is useful biological evidence, but it is not a reason for an individual to request a larger dose than the authorised schedule.

A dose used as an additional primary-series dose for some immunocompromised people is not automatically the same as a routine booster. Product, age, immune status and the schedule in force all affect the correct amount and timing.

Later clinical studies gave a fuller picture than was available in the first reports. The early statement that no firm estimate existed should be read in its historical setting, not repeated as though Moderna has never been studied against Omicron.

Johnson & Johnson: antibody findings and a separate safety decision

Early laboratory findings after a single original Johnson & Johnson/Janssen dose showed limited neutralising activity against Omicron in some assays. That did not establish that every recipient had no immune protection: antibody assays do not capture every component of immunity.

There was also a separate US safety and effectiveness decision. On December 16, 2021, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices recommended preferential use of mRNA vaccines over Janssen for adults. The date was 2021, not December 2020.

That recommendation considered the overall benefit–risk balance, including rare serious adverse events such as thrombosis with thrombocytopenia syndrome. It should not be described as a conclusion drawn solely from one Omicron antibody experiment.

A person who had previously received Janssen needed advice about subsequent recommended doses rather than an assumption that their earlier vaccination was worthless. For anyone with new concerning symptoms, the appropriate response is clinical assessment; a general claim that the danger period has passed cannot replace it.

Mixing vaccine types and what happened to Janssen

Studies of a different vaccine for the booster, sometimes called heterologous boosting, found improved immune responses in several combinations. An mRNA dose after a Janssen primary dose was among the approaches considered during that period.

The evidence that a combination produces a strong antibody response does not by itself authorise every possible combination or timing. Public-health recommendations and product authorisations determine which schedules can be used in a particular setting.

Janssen’s US emergency-use authorisation was revoked on June 1, 2023, following the manufacturer’s request. It therefore should not appear in a current US article as though it remains a routine available choice alongside updated vaccines.

If your vaccination history includes an older product, bring that record to a clinician or vaccination service. They can apply current guidance to the actual doses and dates rather than treating the old article as a schedule.

People with weakened immune systems and children

The first Omicron reports highlighted that breakthrough infections could be more serious in people with weakened immune systems, including some transplant recipients and people receiving chemotherapy. Their vaccine responses and risk can differ from the averages reported for a general study population.

Current CDC guidance uses a modified schedule for people who are moderately or severely immunocompromised, with recommendations depending on age and vaccination history. The treating team may also need to consider the timing of immune-suppressing treatment. Do not stop such treatment or choose additional doses without advice.

The old statement that every US child aged five or older was eligible reflected a particular moment in the rollout. It is not a current eligibility rule. Children’s products, authorised ages, risk-based recommendations and availability must be checked for the relevant country and season.

Adults and parents can ask which current formulation is appropriate, when the next dose is due, and whether medical history changes the plan. Pregnancy or a history of a serious vaccine reaction also merits an individual discussion using current local guidance.

How to use this evidence for a decision now

The virus and vaccine formulations have continued to change since the original Omicron comparisons. In its May 2026 composition statement, WHO retained LP.8.1 as the recommended antigen and also allowed other approaches with suitable evidence. In the United States, FDA advised an XFG formulation for fall 2026.

Those are dated examples of how vaccine composition is reviewed. They do not establish a single worldwide eligibility schedule or mean that a manufacturer’s brand name identifies an unchanged product across all years.

Before relying on a comparison, check the study date, formulation, outcome and time since vaccination. Then check the current recommendations where you live. A pharmacist, vaccination clinic or treating clinician can explain how they apply to your health and previous doses.

The enduring lesson from the early Omicron evidence is that protection against infection and severe illness can change differently, and additional recommended vaccination can improve protection. The specific product and schedule for you should come from current guidance, not a percentage carried forward from 2021.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Early Omicron studies consistently distinguished reduced protection against infection from better-retained protection against serious outcomes. Laboratory neutralisation, modelling and observational effectiveness estimates answer different questions and cannot be treated as interchangeable percentages.

WHO and national regulators continue to review vaccine composition. The 2026 examples below are dated and jurisdiction-specific; eligibility and schedules need a fresh local check before publication or clinical use.

How BeMama can help

Keep vaccination names and dates with your health questions. For a child or a person receiving immune-suppressing treatment, confirm the current schedule with the relevant healthcare team rather than applying an old adult booster comparison.

When to seek help

This is a historical evidence explanation, not a dosing schedule. Product availability, age eligibility and recommendations vary by country and season. Seek personalised advice for immune suppression, pregnancy or a previous serious reaction, and urgent care for severe symptoms.

Evidence notes updated: October 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • The early Omicron comparison belongs to late 2021 and early 2022.
  • Preventing infection and preventing hospitalisation are different outcomes.
  • Antibody fold changes are not clinical effectiveness percentages.
  • Early booster benefits did not establish a permanent three-dose schedule.
  • The old Janssen and age-five advice must not be treated as current guidance.
  • Use current local recommendations for product choice and timing.

Frequently asked questions

Are the 70% and 88% figures current vaccine effectiveness?

No. They describe particular analyses from the first Omicron wave and different study populations or outcomes. They are not current individual guarantees.

Does 70% effectiveness mean 30% of vaccinated people go to hospital?

No. It describes a relative reduction in a measured outcome compared with the study’s comparison group. Absolute risk depends on many other factors.

Can a vaccinated person still catch an Omicron variant?

Yes. Protection against infection is incomplete and changes over time. Protection against serious illness is a different outcome.

Does a 37-fold antibody increase mean 37 times more protection?

No. It is a laboratory measurement relative to a starting level. It cannot be translated directly into a personal clinical protection rate.

Was the early 88% hospitalisation figure specific to Moderna?

No. The cited UK analysis combined vaccine brands. It should not be presented as a fixed Moderna-only result.

Was the US preference for mRNA over Janssen issued in 2020?

No. The relevant ACIP recommendation was made on December 16, 2021.

Is Janssen still a routine US vaccine option?

Its US emergency-use authorisation was revoked on June 1, 2023. Use current local information about available products.

Should I choose the higher Moderna dose mentioned in old studies?

No. Experimental antibody comparisons do not determine your dose. The authorised product and current schedule must match age, medical history and local guidance.

Should every child follow the old age-five recommendation?

No. That statement reflected an earlier rollout. Current age eligibility, formulations and risk recommendations need to be checked locally.

What should someone with a weakened immune system do?

Ask the treating team or vaccination service to review current guidance alongside previous doses and treatment timing. A general adult schedule may not apply.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
